title: PHYS 200 - Lecture 16 - The Taylor Series and Other Mathematical Concepts

source.credit: Lecture: Prof. Ramamurti Shankar, Fundamentals of Physics I (PHYS 200), Open Yale Courses, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0

cards.quote: If x is small enough you stop there, because the next time it's going to involve an x2 and an x3, then if x is tiny, we have no respect for x2 and x3, we just cut it off.
If you expand this in a power series, you're going to get mc2 + ½ mv2, plus stuff involving v to the 4th over c to the 4th times c2.
cards.plain: The expansion contains the classical kinetic energy ½mv².

cards.quote: This is 1 minus x2 over 2, looks like this.
And we would like to write it as follows: d2x over dt2 is equal to minus ω2 x, where ω is the shorthand for squared root of k over m.
cards.plain: A mass-spring oscillator has angular frequency √(k/m).

cards.quote: If the spring is very stiff and k is very large, frequency is very high.
cards.plain: Increasing spring stiffness increases the oscillation frequency.

cards.quote: If the mass is very big and the motion is very sluggish, f is diminished.
cards.plain: Increasing mass decreases the oscillation frequency.

cards.quote: You are told whether you pull the spring by one inch or by ten inches, the time it takes to finish a full back and forth motion is independent of A.
cards.plain: The spring's period is independent of its amplitude.

cards.quote: This frequency here is independent of A.
cards.plain: The spring's frequency is independent of amplitude.

cards.quote: So, the remarkable property of simple harmonic motion is that the amplitude does not determine the time period.
cards.plain: Amplitude does not determine the harmonic oscillator's period.

cards.quote: On the other hand, no matter how much you pulled it and how you released it, this ω, and therefore the frequency, are not variable.
cards.plain: Initial displacement and release do not change frequency.

cards.quote: Even though position and velocity are constantly changing, this combination, if you crank it out, will not depend on time.
cards.plain: The oscillator's kinetic plus potential energy is constant.

cards.quote: So, for small angles, sin θ is θ, and the restoring torque, in fact, is linear in the angle of the coordinate.
cards.plain: For small angles, sin θ ≈ θ.

cards.quote: So, you find ω is equal to square root of g over l, and that is 2π over T.
cards.plain: A small-angle pendulum has angular frequency √(g/l).

cards.quote: So, you get back the famous formula you learned, T is 2π square root of l over g.
What that means is, if you took a real pendulum with a massless rod and a bob at the end, the time it takes to finish an oscillation, in fact, will depend on the amplitude.
cards.plain: A real pendulum's period depends on amplitude.

cards.quote: But only for small oscillations, when sin θ can be approximated by θ, you will find whether you do that the time is the same.
cards.plain: For small oscillations, pendulum period is amplitude-independent.

cards.quote: The period of a pendulum, in fact, is not just a function of l and g, but also a function of the amplitude.
cards.plain: Pendulum period also depends on amplitude.

skipped.quote: So, the next lesson of our Taylor series is, you can write down the series, but it may not sum up to anything sensible beyond a certain range.
skipped.why: no library rule for Taylor-series convergence

skipped.quote: Newtonian mechanics works for small velocities.
skipped.why: no library rule for the general validity of Newtonian mechanics

skipped.quote: That's something I'm not proving, but the series for ex, no limits on validity.
skipped.why: no library rule for convergence of the exponential series

skipped.quote: It's a ubiquitous fact, that if you took any mechanical system which is in a state of equilibrium, and you give it a little kick, it vibrates.
skipped.why: no library rule for arbitrary mechanical systems

skipped.quote: If you tamper with this, if you add to this a little bit, like 1 over 100 times x3, then all these bets are off.
skipped.why: no library rule varying nonlinear spring stiffness

skipped.quote: So, that's the energy of an oscillator, ½ kA2.
skipped.why: no library rule for total oscillator energy

skipped.quote: So, center of mass of a body need not lie on the body.
skipped.why: no library rule for center of mass
